title: The dark night
hook: John of the Cross wrote of a dark night where prayer feels empty and something deeper grows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's interior castle: a soul of many rooms, with prayer as the door. Your line was many rooms.

For years, morning prayer was the best part of her day. Warm. Easy. Words came. Today, nothing. Not anger, not doubt exactly. Just flat, like chewing paper. Tomorrow, the same. And the next week. She starts to wonder what she's done wrong. Teresa's friend and fellow Carmelite, a friar called John of the Cross, wrote a poem about a night like that, and then a whole book explaining the poem. His surprising claim is that the flatness might not mean something has gone wrong at all.
screen: `IT USED TO BE EASY.` → `TODAY, NOTHING.` → `MAYBE NOTHING'S GONE WRONG.`

segments.voice: John's poem begins on a dark night, with someone slipping out of a quiet house, unseen, to meet the one they love. The night isn't the enemy; later in the poem, it's the guide. His prose book, The Dark Night, explains what that means for prayer. First, the sweetness goes. Beginners, John says, often find prayer full of comfort, and then, for a time, God takes the comfort away. The old ways of praying, with pictures and thoughts, stop working. Second, it isn't every dark mood. He gives signs to tell this night apart from ordinary sadness, or what he calls melancholy. The person finds no pleasure in God's things, but none in other things either. They still care, painfully, about whether they're serving God. And they can't meditate with the imagination the way they used to. Third, what to do. John's advice is gentle: don't strain to force the old feelings back. Rest in peace and quiet, with a simple loving attention, even if it seems like wasting time. Fourth, what grows. In John's reading, the night strips away a love that depended on good feelings, so that something quieter and deeper can grow underneath. Some today say dark night of the soul for any hard time; John's own night is narrower, and he took care to say not every darkness is this one. Hard seasons that weigh on everything deserve a friend, and sometimes a doctor, as well as a prayer. If a weight ever feels like too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
screen: `THE NIGHT IS THE GUIDE.` · `THE SWEETNESS GOES.` · `NOT EVERY DARK MOOD.` · `REST IN LOVING ATTENTION.` · then: `IF IT'S HEAVY: 988, OR LOCAL HELP.`

segments.voice: Think of a time when something you loved went flat: a prayer, a friendship, a craft, a job. Don't try to fix it or to feel anything special; just sit beside it, the way you'd sit with a friend who doesn't need advice. If you pray, you can offer the dryness itself, without words; if not, just keep it company.
The dark night. In John of the Cross, a season when prayer goes flat and the old comforts fall away, and something quieter grows underneath. Today's word.
Your line: a dark night. Flat isn't always a sign that something's gone wrong. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Christians who meet dryness in prayer often talk it over with a spiritual director, who may draw on John of the Cross to help tell a dark night apart from depression or ordinary discouragement.

chat.says: Prayer used to feel warm, and now it feels flat. Did I do something wrong?
options: Not necessarily. John of the Cross says old comforts can fade while something deeper grows.
Yes. Flat prayer always means you've drifted from God and must try much harder.
No. It just means prayer was never real, so it's time to stop praying at all.
chat.meaning: John of the Cross taught that the night can strip away a love that leaned on good feelings, so something quieter grows. He advised resting in loving attention.
